topics.title: How the web works
topics.technical: A browser resolves a domain through DNS, opens a TLS connection, and sends an HTTP request; a server answers with HTML the browser parses into the DOM, fetching CSS, JavaScript and images as it discovers them. Every performance and security decision hangs off this request/response skeleton.
topics.simple: Type an address, and your browser asks a server for a page, then assembles the pieces it receives into what you see.

topics.title: HTML: the structure
topics.technical: HTML marks meaning, not looks: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images and forms nest into a tree. Semantic elements — nav, main, article, footer — tell browsers, screen readers and search engines what each region is, which is why div-soup is a defect, not a style.
topics.simple: HTML is the skeleton of every page: what things ARE — a heading, a list, a button — not how they look.

topics.title: Forms and inputs
topics.technical: Forms collect user data with typed inputs — email, number, date — whose built-in validation (required, pattern, min) runs before any JavaScript. Labels bind text to controls for accessibility, and method/action decide how the browser submits without a single script.
topics.simple: Forms are how users talk back. The browser already knows how to check emails and require fields — use it before writing code.

topics.title: CSS: selectors and the cascade
topics.technical: CSS rules select elements and declare properties; conflicts resolve by specificity, then source order, with inheritance filling gaps. The box model — content, padding, border, margin — governs all sizing, and box-sizing: border-box makes it sane.
topics.simple: CSS paints the skeleton. When two rules argue, the more specific and later one wins — that argument is the cascade.

topics.title: Layout: Flexbox
topics.technical: Flexbox lays out one dimension at a time: a flex container distributes space among children with justify-content and align-items, wraps with flex-wrap, and reorders visually without touching the HTML. It replaced float hacks for almost every component-level layout.
topics.simple: Flexbox lines things up in a row or column and shares out the spare space — the everyday layout tool.

topics.title: Layout: Grid
topics.technical: CSS Grid is two-dimensional: define rows and columns (fr units, minmax, auto-fit), then place children into areas by name or line. Page-level scaffolding — header, sidebar, content, footer — is Grid's home turf, with Flexbox for what lives inside.
topics.simple: Grid draws the page's chessboard — rows AND columns — and drops each piece exactly where you name.

topics.title: Responsive design
topics.technical: Responsive pages adapt with fluid units (%, rem, vw), media queries at content-driven breakpoints, and responsive images via srcset. Mobile-first CSS starts narrow and layers width on top; the meta viewport tag is the one line without which phones lie about their size.
topics.simple: One page, every screen: measure in relative units, adjust at sensible widths, and design for the phone first.

topics.title: JavaScript: the language
topics.technical: JavaScript brings behaviour: let/const scoping, first-class functions, closures, objects and arrays with rich methods (map, filter, reduce), and template literals. It runs single-threaded inside the page — everything interactive on the web ends up here.
topics.simple: JavaScript is the muscle of a page: the language that reacts, computes and changes what you see.

topics.title: The DOM: scripting the page
topics.technical: The DOM is the page as live objects: querySelector finds nodes, textContent and classList change them, createElement and append grow the tree. Every visual change a user sees is a DOM mutation something scripted.
topics.simple: The page is a tree your code can climb and prune: find an element, change its text, add a class, insert a new branch.

topics.title: Events
topics.technical: addEventListener subscribes handlers to clicks, input, keys and scroll; events bubble up the tree, so one listener on a parent can serve a thousand children (delegation). preventDefault stops native behaviour, and the event object carries everything about what happened.
topics.simple: Events are the page's nervous system: something happens, your function fires, one listener can watch a whole region.

topics.title: Async JavaScript: promises and fetch
topics.technical: JavaScript never waits: slow operations return promises, consumed with async/await inside try/catch. fetch performs HTTP from the page, res.json() parses answers, and the event loop explains why nothing blocks while everything appears sequential.
topics.simple: The page fetches data in the background and your code says 'await' — wait here, but keep the page alive meanwhile.

topics.title: Working with APIs and JSON
topics.technical: Front ends live on JSON APIs: request with the right method and headers, check response.ok before parsing, render data into the DOM, and show honest loading and error states. The contract with the server — the shapes exchanged — is the real interface of your app.
topics.simple: Your page asks servers for data and draws the answers. Good pages also show 'loading' and admit failures.

topics.title: Browser storage and state
topics.technical: localStorage persists small key-value strings per origin; sessionStorage forgets on close; cookies travel to the server with every request. JSON.stringify bridges objects to storage, and nothing secret belongs in any of them — the user can read every byte.
topics.simple: The browser can remember for you — preferences, drafts, a token — but anything stored there, the user can see.

topics.title: Accessibility
topics.technical: Accessibility is engineering, not garnish: semantic elements and labels give assistive tech a map, keyboard operability covers every interaction, focus is visible and managed, contrast meets WCAG ratios, and ARIA fills only the gaps semantics cannot. Broken a11y excludes real users.
topics.simple: The web is for everyone: keyboards must reach everything, screen readers must understand everything, contrast must be readable.

topics.title: Git and deployment for the front end
topics.technical: Front-end work ships through the same git flow as everything else, and static hosting deploys it: push to a repo, a pipeline builds, a CDN serves. HTTPS, caching headers and atomic deploys come free from the platform; a URL anyone can open is the definition of done.
topics.simple: Your page is not real until it is on the internet: git push, automatic build, live URL.

topics.title: React: components and JSX
topics.technical: React describes UI as components — functions returning JSX — and re-renders them when data changes, reconciling the DOM for you. Props flow data down, composition builds screens from parts, and thinking in components replaces thinking in pages.
topics.simple: React lets you build the page out of Lego bricks you design, and it repaints them automatically when data changes.

topics.title: React state and hooks
topics.technical: useState holds component state whose setter triggers re-render; useEffect runs side effects after render with a dependency array governing when. Lifting state up shares it between siblings, and the rules of hooks — top level only — keep the machinery deterministic.
topics.simple: State is what a component remembers. Change it through the setter and React redraws exactly what depends on it.

topics.title: React forms, lists and effects in practice
topics.technical: Controlled inputs bind form fields to state; lists render with map and stable keys; data loads in effects with loading and error states modelled explicitly. These three patterns compose into nearly every screen a working front end ships.
topics.simple: Forms, lists and fetched data — the three patterns almost every real screen is built from.

topics.title: Routing and multi-page apps
topics.technical: Client-side routing swaps components on URL changes without full reloads: routes declare the map, links navigate, params carry ids, and a catch-all route handles the unknown. The URL is state — a screen you cannot link to is a screen users cannot share.
topics.simple: One app pretending to be many pages: the address bar changes, React swaps the view, and every screen is shareable.

topics.title: Performance and DevTools
topics.technical: DevTools exposes the truth: the Network tab shows what loads and how slowly, Lighthouse scores what matters, and the Performance panel finds jank. Optimise by measurement — compress images, lazy-load below the fold, cache aggressively — never by folklore.
topics.simple: The browser's built-in X-ray shows why a page is slow; fix what the measurements name, not what you guess.

topics.title: The final project
topics.technical: Ship a complete responsive React application against a real API: routed screens, forms with validation, loading and error states, accessibility passes, deployed to a public URL with the repo README explaining it. This is the portfolio piece that opens interviews.
topics.simple: One finished, live, responsive app that uses everything above — with a link you can put on a resume.
